title: Distributed Cron & Delayed Job Scheduler (At-Least-Once Delivery)
businessContext: A subscription and billing platform executes millions of scheduled tasks: daily recurring billing crons, delayed subscription trial expiry emails (execute 14 days after signup), and abandoned cart nudges (execute in 2 hours). The current single-server cron daemon is a single point of failure and misses jobs during restarts.
problemStatement: Design a horizontally scalable, fault-tolerant distributed cron and delayed task scheduling service. The system must guarantee at-least-once task execution, support dynamic schedules (run at exact timestamp T), scale worker nodes horizontally, support graceful retries with dead-letter queues, and prevent duplicate concurrent task execution.
constraints: Scale: 10,000,000 scheduled tasks stored, 10,000 tasks dispatched per second.
Precision: Jobs must trigger within +/- 1 second of their scheduled target timestamp.
High Availability: Zero dropped jobs if any scheduler node crashes.

systemDesignReqs.scale: 10M scheduled tasks, 10k triggers/sec peak, 50 worker instances.
functional: Schedule one-time delayed task (run at timestamp T).
Support job cancellation, status inspection, and execution history.
Configurable retry policies with dead-letter queues.
nonFunctional: High availability with leader election or leaderless partitioned dispatch.
assumptions: Jobs are defined with idempotency keys so workers can safely handle at-least-once delivery.

candidateTasks: Design the architecture: Scheduler Fleet, Time-Wheel / Redis Sorted Set / DynamoDB Time-Partitioned Storage, Dispatch Queue (SQS / Kafka / RabbitMQ), Worker Fleet.
Explain how Redis Sorted Set (`ZADD scheduled_time taskId`, `ZRANGEBYSCORE 0 now`) or Hashed Time-Wheels dispatch due tasks.
Explain how distributed locking or partitioned ranges prevent multiple scheduler nodes from dispatching the same due task.
Detail the worker execution lease and heartbeating mechanism.
hints: Use Redis Sorted Sets (ZSET) where score = scheduled Unix timestamp in milliseconds.
Use Lua script or `ZPOPMIN` to atomically retrieve and remove due tasks so schedulers don't double-dispatch.
alternativeApproaches: Hierarchical Hashed Timing Wheels (Kafka / Netty approach) for sub-millisecond precision.
Using managed services like AWS EventBridge Scheduler or Google Cloud Tasks.
commonMistakes: Polling a relational database table with `SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE run_at <= NOW()`: under millions of rows and frequent polling, this causes table lock contention and index thrashing.
Failing to make worker tasks idempotent: in distributed systems, at-least-once delivery guarantees that occasional duplicate deliveries WILL happen.
